case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 10 U.S.C. § 1413a (Combat-Related Special Compensation) supplies its own claim-settlement scheme that displaces the federal default claim-settlement and time-bar rules in the Barring Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3702, for CRSC payment claims.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 10 U.S.C. § 1413a and 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A) (the Barring Act’s coverage of claims "involving ... retired pay" and its default settlement/time-limitation framework).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Soto argues that once the Federal Circuit categorized CRSC as a claim "involving ... retired pay" under the Barring Act, the next step is to apply this Court’s displacement framework: because § 1413a creates a specific, self-contained mechanism for determining eligibility and paying CRSC (a specialized statutory benefits program administered within DoD), that specific scheme should control over the Barring Act’s default settlement procedures and limitations. Petitioner contends the Federal Circuit erred by treating the Barring Act as governing despite § 1413a’s tailored process, thereby improperly limiting or channeling veterans’ CRSC entitlement claims under a general claims-settlement statute.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues the Barring Act provides the comprehensive, default settlement regime for monetary claims against the government—including those involving military retired pay—and § 1413a does not clearly establish an alternative settlement mechanism sufficient to displace that default. In the government’s view, § 1413a authorizes and defines the benefit but does not create the kind of explicit, comprehensive claim-settlement and limitations structure that would override § 3702; therefore, Barring Act procedures and constraints continue to apply to CRSC-related monetary claims.
key_precedents: No specific Supreme Court precedents are identified by name in the excerpts provided; the parties reference "this Court’s precedent" governing when a later, specific statutory scheme displaces the Barring Act’s default framework.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that § 1413a directs DoD to determine eligibility, calculate CRSC, and pay it—so importing § 3702 risks limiting a remedial veterans’ program. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 1413a does not speak in the procedural register of presentment, settlement authority, finality, or a limitations period; § 3702 does, and it expressly covers claims “involving … retired pay,” making it the default unless Congress clearly provides “another provision of law” that displaces it. Illinois Surety reinforces that “settlement” is a distinct, final administrative determination on a monetary claim, and § 1413a’s benefit-administration directions are not a comprehensive, exclusive settlement-and-time-bar regime. Under a minimalist approach mindful of institutional legitimacy, we should not infer an implied carveout from a governmentwide Treasury-protective framework absent unmistakable textual direction from Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that § 1413a directs DoD to determine eligibility and calculate CRSC, so importing § 3702’s six-year presentment bar may seem redundant and unduly harsh in a remedial scheme. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch stress, that policy intuition cannot overcome the texts: § 3702 expressly establishes a governmentwide settlement-and-time-bar rule for any claim “involving … retired pay,” while § 1413a contains no unmistakable displacement signals—no exclusive settlement authority, presentment rule, finality provision, or limitations period. Illinois Surety’s understanding of “settlement” as a distinct, final administrative determination of the amount due supports treating § 1413a as creating the substantive entitlement and payment administration, while § 3702 supplies the default procedures and timeliness rules for retroactive money demands against the United States. Under an original public meaning approach, absent a clear contrary directive, we apply the general claims-processing statute as written and leave any veteran-specific carveout to Congress.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that § 1413a directs DoD to determine eligibility, calculate CRSC, and pay it—so, in a functional sense, it looks like a complete administrative mechanism and importing § 3702 could work hardship on deserving veterans. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 3702 is written as a governmentwide default for monetary claims “involving … retired pay,” and § 1413a does not speak in the distinctive procedural terms Congress uses when it means to displace that default (presentment, settlement authority, finality, and a limitations rule). Illinois Surety’s understanding of “settlement” as a distinct, final administrative determination on a presented monetary claim reinforces that eligibility/payment administration under § 1413a is not the same thing as a substitute settlement-and-time-bar regime. Under a textualist approach attentive to administrability and protection of the Treasury, any veteran-specific carveout from § 3702 must be made expressly by Congress, not inferred from § 1413a’s remedial purpose.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that § 3702 is a governmentwide default and we should not infer displacement without clear textual markers (presentment, finality, limitations), especially given Illinois Surety’s account of “settlement” as a final administrative determination. But Illinois Surety cuts against Respondent’s framing here: if “settlement” is about who makes the operative administrative determination of the amount due, § 1413a assigns that core function to DoD—eligibility, computation, and payment—so importing GAO’s overlay (and its six-year bar) is not merely “coexistence,” it is a substantive restriction on a remedial benefit Congress entrusted to the administering agency. Under my pragmatic, access-to-justice lens, the absence of an express limitations period in a veteran-protective statute is a poor basis to impose a separate, Treasury-protective time bar that predictably defeats meritorious claims due to delay, disability, or lack of notice rather than lack of entitlement. I therefore continue to read § 1413a as the more specific, self-contained remedial scheme that should control over § 3702 in this context, notwithstanding Justice Roberts’s administrability concerns.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument is that § 1413a already assigns DoD the job of determining eligibility, calculating CRSC, and paying it—functionally a kind of "settlement"—so importing § 3702’s presentment bar could undercut a targeted remedial scheme. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 3702 addresses a different, explicitly procedural question—how monetary claims against the United States are presented, settled with finality, and time-barred—and § 1413a lacks the distinct markers (presentment, finality, exclusivity, limitations) that would signal displacement rather than coexistence. Illinois Surety matters here because it underscores that “settlement” is a specialized term for the administrative resolution of claims against the Treasury; § 1413a’s benefit-administration directions can be read to create entitlement and prospective payments without clearly providing a substitute, comprehensive claims-processing regime for retroactive underpayment disputes. On my pragmatic textualist view, the more workable, coherent reading is that § 1413a and § 3702 operate on different planes—substantive entitlement vs. governmentwide claim presentment and timeliness—absent an unmistakable statutory instruction to carve CRSC out of § 3702.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress that § 1413a requires DoD to determine eligibility, calculate CRSC, and pay it, but that kind of benefits administration still is not what § 3702 (as understood in Illinois Surety) calls “settlement”—a distinct, final administrative determination of a monetary claim presented against the United States, coupled with an express presentment-and-time-bar regime. As Justice Barrett explains, the specific-over-general canon does not apply absent a true conflict; § 1413a can supply the substantive entitlement and payment mechanics while § 3702 supplies the governmentwide default rules for when and how underpayment claims “involving … retired pay” must be presented and are barred. I also agree with the Chief Justice that displacement of a Treasury-protective, governmentwide claims-processing framework ordinarily requires clear textual signals (presentment, finality, exclusivity, limitations), which § 1413a lacks. Whatever the equities for combat-disabled retirees, under a textualist/originalist approach that is a matter for Congress to address expressly rather than for us to infer by implication.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that § 1413a’s eligibility, calculation, and payment directions amount to “settlement” under Illinois Surety—does not persuade me because § 3702 uses “settlement” as a distinct claims-presentment and final administrative resolution mechanism coupled to an express six-year bar, and § 1413a lacks any comparable, self-contained timeliness/finality framework for retroactive underpayment demands. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, we should require a clear congressional signal before displacing a governmentwide Treasury-protective default for claims “involving … retired pay,” and inferring ouster from program administration alone risks undermining uniformity and administrability. Justice Kagan’s coherence point is also important: § 1413a can define the entitlement while § 3702 governs the separate question of how and when monetary claims against the United States must be presented and are time-barred, so there is no true conflict triggering specific-over-general displacement. The remedial equities are real, but under an institutionalist, precedent- and text-centered approach, that policy concern cannot substitute for the unmistakable statutory direction Congress typically provides when it intends a carveout from § 3702.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that § 1413a directs DoD to determine eligibility, calculate CRSC, and pay it—functions that can resemble an administrative “determination of the amount due.” But even accepting Illinois Surety’s understanding of “settlement,” § 3702 does more than identify an agency that can compute amounts; it supplies an integrated claims-processing regime (presentment, settlement authority, finality, and a six-year bar) for monetary claims “involving … retired pay,” and § 1413a contains no comparably “precisely drawn” replacement. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the specific-over-general canon requires an actual conflict in operative commands; here the statutes sensibly coexist because § 1413a creates and administers the entitlement while § 3702 governs when retroactive underpayment demands against the United States must be presented and are time-barred. The equities Justice Sotomayor raises are serious, but under a textualist/originalist approach they cannot justify inferring displacement of a governmentwide timeliness rule absent clearer congressional direction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s fairness-and-tailoring point has real force: CRSC is a targeted remedial program, and a six-year presentment bar can functionally deny relief to disabled veterans who lacked notice or faced bureaucratic delay. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, § 3702 is Congress’s express, governmentwide settlement-and-timeliness regime for monetary claims “involving … retired pay,” and § 1413a does not speak in the procedural register (presentment, finality, limitations) that would clearly displace that default. Illinois Surety’s understanding of “settlement” as a distinct final administrative determination of amount due supports treating § 3702 as governing underpayment claims even when § 1413a supplies the substantive entitlement and internal eligibility/calculation steps. Under my pragmatic methodology, the remedial purpose matters, but absent clearer congressional direction I cannot infer an implicit carveout from a Treasury-protective, uniform claims-processing statute based on program specificity alone.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Barring Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3702, establishes the default, comprehensive administrative settlement and presentment regime for monetary claims against the United States—including claims “involving ... retired pay,” § 3702(a)(1)(A)—unless another statute clearly provides its own settlement mechanism. Although 10 U.S.C. § 1413a authorizes CRSC and directs DoD to determine eligibility and calculate payments, it does not speak in the kind of clear, comprehensive, and exclusive terms that would displace § 3702’s settlement/time-bar framework, particularly given Congress’s choice not to supply a distinct limitations rule. Consistent with judicial minimalism and respect for established default rules governing claims against the Treasury, I would not infer displacement from an entitlement statute absent unmistakable direction from Congress. Illinois Surety Co. v. United States, 240 U.S. 214, 219 (1916), supports treating “settlement” as the final administrative determination of liability and reinforces that § 3702 applies unless another law expressly covers settlement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Barring Act applies to any claim “involving … retired pay,” 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A), and it supplies the default administrative settlement and time-bar rules unless another statute provides a clearly exclusive settlement mechanism. Section 1413a authorizes and defines CRSC eligibility and directs payment by the Secretary concerned, but it does not textually create a comprehensive claims-settlement and limitations regime that displaces § 3702’s general framework. Under the traditional presumption that Congress does not impliedly repeal or displace a generally applicable statutory scheme absent clear indication, the specific-benefit authorization in § 1413a is not enough to override the Barring Act’s settlement/time-bar rules. Because the text does not clearly establish an alternative settlement scheme, § 3702 governs CRSC payment claims.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Barring Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A), by its terms supplies a default settlement and time-bar regime for monetary claims against the United States “involving … retired pay,” and CRSC claims fall within that category once classified as such. Nothing in 10 U.S.C. § 1413a clearly provides an alternative, comprehensive claim-settlement and limitations framework that Congress intended to displace § 3702; it authorizes and defines eligibility and payment administration, but does not expressly override the Barring Act’s settlement authority or six-year bar. Under this Court’s understanding that “settlement” means an administrative determination of the amount due, § 1413a’s benefit-administration provisions do not amount to the kind of explicit, self-contained settlement scheme necessary to supplant the governmentwide default. Given the practical consequences for uniform administration of federal pay claims, displacement should require clear congressional direction, which is absent here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3702 operates as a default administrative settlement and time-bar regime only where another statute does not provide a mechanism to determine and pay the amount due, and this Court has understood “settlement” in this context as “the administrative determination of the amount due” on a demand for payment. 10 U.S.C. § 1413a is a targeted veterans’ benefits program administered within DoD that specifies eligibility, calculation, and payment of CRSC, thereby supplying the very type of claim-determination procedure that should displace the Barring Act’s general framework, including its six-year limitation. Reading § 3702 to impose an extra, general-claims overlay on top of Congress’s tailored remedial scheme risks unfairly cutting off relief for medically retired, combat-disabled veterans—precisely the kind of vulnerable population Congress sought to protect by expanding CRSC in 2008. Absent a clearer congressional directive that § 3702’s time bar governs these benefit determinations, the specific statute (§ 1413a) should control over the general default settlement statute (§ 3702(a)(1)(A)).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3702 supplies the Government’s default, comprehensive claim-settlement and time-bar regime for monetary claims “involving … retired pay,” 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A), and displacement requires a clear alternative “settlement” scheme. Although 10 U.S.C. § 1413a establishes eligibility and directs DoD to administer CRSC, it does not speak with the kind of explicitness and comprehensiveness about claim presentment, settlement authority, and finality that would clearly oust § 3702’s default framework, so the two provisions can operate coherently together. Under ordinary textual canons, the court should not infer displacement or rewrite the enacted allocation of settlement authority and limitations where Congress did not clearly provide it. See Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337, 340 (1997), and United States v. Locke, 471 U.S. 84, 95 (1985).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Barring Act establishes a default, government-wide claim-settlement and timeliness regime for claims “involving ... retired pay,” 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A), and displacement requires a clear textual indication that Congress supplied an alternative, exclusive settlement scheme. Section 1413a authorizes and defines CRSC eligibility and directs DoD administration, but it does not speak in the sort of comprehensive, exclusivity-bearing terms (settlement authority, finality, and a limitations rule) that would displace § 3702’s otherwise applicable rules. Under the plain-meaning canon that the specific governs the general only when the statutes conflict, see Nat’l Cable & Telecommunications Ass’n v. Gulf Power Co., 534 U.S. 327, 335 (2002), there is no necessary conflict here: § 1413a can create the benefit while § 3702 supplies the default settlement/time bar for monetary claims against the United States. And consistent with the understanding of “settle” as a final administrative determination of liability, Illinois Surety Co. v. United States, 240 U.S. 214, 219 (1916), § 1413a lacks the indicia of a self-contained settlement and time-bar framework that would override Congress’s general claims-processing statute.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Barring Act supplies a comprehensive default administrative settlement regime for monetary claims against the United States, including claims “involving … retired pay,” and it applies unless “another provision of law” provides its own settlement mechanism. 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A), (b)(1). Although 10 U.S.C. § 1413a creates and administers the CRSC benefit, it does not clearly establish a separate, self-contained claim-settlement and limitations framework that displaces § 3702’s settlement authority and six-year presentment bar; absent that kind of clear statutory displacement, the Court should adhere to the default regime Congress enacted in § 3702 for workability and uniformity. Consistent with the Court’s understanding that “settlement” refers to a final administrative determination of the amount due, Illinois Sur. Co. v. United States, 240 U.S. 214, 219 (1916), § 3702’s structure more directly addresses settlement and timing than § 1413a’s benefit-eligibility provisions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Barring Act establishes a default, comprehensive settlement and time-bar regime for “claim[s] … involving … retired pay,” 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A), and CRSC payment claims fall within that textual category. Nothing in 10 U.S.C. § 1413a supplies a comparably “precisely drawn, detailed” alternative claim-settlement scheme—§ 1413a defines eligibility and authorizes payments but does not set out an express settlement authority, limitations period, or an integrated administrative adjudication framework that would displace § 3702’s generally applicable rules. Applying the specific-over-general canon requires a genuine conflict between the two statutes’ operative instructions, and here § 1413a can operate alongside § 3702 because it creates the benefit while § 3702 governs how monetary claims against the United States are settled and time-barred. Under this Court’s approach in United States v. Babcock, displacement is not inferred from program specificity alone; Congress must speak with sufficient clarity to supplant the default settlement statute, which § 1413a does not do.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3702(a)(1)(A) expressly provides the default administrative “settlement” and time-bar regime for monetary claims “involving ... retired pay,” and nothing in 10 U.S.C. § 1413a clearly supplies a comparable, self-contained claim-settlement or limitations framework for retroactive underpayment disputes. While § 1413a defines eligibility and directs the Secretary to make monthly CRSC payments, that looks like a substantive benefits authorization, not a displacement of Congress’s general claims-processing statute; reading implicit displacement here risks undermining § 3702’s allocation of settlement authority over military pay-related claims. Consistent with this Court’s understanding of “settlement” as an administrative determination of the amount due, the Barring Act fills the procedural gap for adjudicating and time-limiting underpayment demands unless Congress clearly indicates otherwise. Given the practical consequences, channeling these disputes through an established, uniform settlement framework promotes evenhanded administration while leaving Congress free to create an explicit alternative if it wishes.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 10 U.S.C. § 1413a supplies its own settlement mechanism for Combat-Related Special Compensation (CRSC) claims that displaces the default settlement procedures and limitations (including time limits) of the Barring Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3702, once the claim is deemed to involve “retired pay.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: 10 U.S.C. § 1413a (Combat-Related Special Compensation) and 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A) (the Barring Act’s settlement authority and limitations for claims involving “retired pay”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Because § 1413a creates a specific, self-contained CRSC claim-and-review process (including who decides eligibility and what procedures apply), it qualifies as a statute that provides its own settlement mechanism and therefore displaces the Barring Act’s default settlement regime; the Federal Circuit erred by treating the Barring Act as governing even though § 1413a itself establishes how CRSC entitlements are determined and corrected.
case_analysis.respondent_position: CRSC claims are claims involving military retired pay and thus fall within the Barring Act’s coverage; § 1413a does not clearly provide a comprehensive alternative ‘settlement mechanism’ that overrides the Barring Act’s default settlement procedures and limitations, so the Barring Act continues to govern the processing and timeliness of such monetary claims against the United States.
key_precedents: Soto v. United States, 92 F.4th 1094 (Fed. Cir. 2024)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s best point remains the conditional trigger in § 3702(b)(1)—claims must be “presented under this section”—and Justice Barrett reinforces that § 1413a creates a distinct departmental process. But I agree with Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh that § 3702(a)(1)(A)’s subject-matter assignment (“claims involving … retired pay”) is the gateway rule, and § 1413a does not clearly “otherwise provide” a substitute limitations/claims-processing regime; it supplies administrators and eligibility/amount criteria, not an express displacement of the governmentwide timeliness rule. Under Babcock’s caution against finding displacement in fiscal/claims statutes by implication, it is more faithful to harmonize: DoD determines entitlement and computes CRSC, while § 3702 supplies the default presentment bar for monetary claims in this class. The petitioner’s reading would effectively treat silence in § 1413a as authorizing open-ended retroactive liability, a step I am not prepared to take without a clearer directive from Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett press the best textual point: § 3702(b)(1) applies only to claims “presented under this section,” and § 1413a routes CRSC through a department-administered process. But in light of § 3702(a)(1)(A)’s subject-matter assignment to “settle” claims involving “retired pay,” the ordinary public meaning is that this class of monetary claims is governed by § 3702’s settlement regime unless Congress clearly “otherwise provide[s]” a substitute, and § 1413a does not supply a limitations rule or an exclusivity directive. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Babcock reinforces that we should not infer displacement of a governmentwide presentment/timeliness rule from statutory silence, especially in fiscal statutes, and harmonization is straightforward: DoD decides eligibility/amount under § 1413a, while § 3702(b)(1) supplies the default presentment bar for the claim as one “under” the settlement statute Congress assigned to retired-pay claims. The petitioners’ approach effectively treats “presented under” as purely forum-dependent, allowing Congress’s general time bar to be evaded by routing, which is not a textualist reading of how § 3702 defines the governance of the underlying claim category.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s textual point that § 3702(b)(1) applies only to claims “presented under this section” is the strongest argument for Petitioner, but it treats § 3702(a)(1)(A)’s subject-matter assignment—claims involving “retired pay”—as if it were optional whenever another statute creates an internal administrative process. As the Chief Justice explains with Babcock, the “except as otherwise provided by law” clause calls for a clear alternative limitations/claims-processing scheme before we infer displacement of a governmentwide presentment bar, and § 1413a is silent on timeliness and does not clearly make DoD’s process exclusive of § 3702’s settlement/timeliness framework. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s view that § 1413a performs “settlement” in a colloquial sense does not answer the fiscal-statute presumption: Congress knows how to authorize open-ended retroactive monetary liability and did not do so here. The better harmonization remains that DoD determines eligibility and computes CRSC under § 1413a, while § 3702 supplies the generally applicable six-year presentment constraint for monetary claims involving retired pay.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s best point is the Babcock-inflected caution against treating § 1413a as an implicit carveout from § 3702’s governmentwide regime, especially given § 1413a’s silence on timeliness. But that caution has less force where § 3702 itself is expressly residual—“except as otherwise provided by law”—and § 1413a does “otherwise provide” by assigning the service Secretaries the operative eligibility-and-amount determination that functions as the relevant “settlement,” making it odd to reimpose § 3702’s separate presentment machinery. Justice Alito’s fiscal-exposure concern is not a textual hook to expand § 3702(b)(1) beyond its trigger (“presented under this section”), and adopting the Respondents’ harmonization effectively imports a limitations bar into a targeted remedial program for combat-injured retirees without Congress saying so. On my pragmatic approach, the real-world consequence—foreclosing benefits based on a procedural bar not clearly attached to this statutory track—confirms we should not read § 3702 to restrict access absent clearer congressional direction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s Babcock-based point—that “except as otherwise provided by law” requires a clear substitute and that § 1413a is silent on timeliness—lands as a serious caution against implied displacement, but it doesn’t answer the narrower textual trigger he must satisfy: § 3702(b)(1) applies only to claims “presented under this section.” As Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett emphasize, CRSC applications are presented through § 1413a’s Secretary-administered process that determines eligibility and computes the amount due—the core “settlement” function—so it is difficult, as a matter of ordinary statutory usage, to deem those claims “presented under” § 3702. Justice Thomas’s effort to read § 3702(a)(1)(A)’s subject-matter grant as pulling § 1413a claims into § 3702(b) effectively severs the limitations clause from its own presentment condition and turns “except as otherwise provided by law” into surplusage when Congress has in fact “otherwise provided” a specific adjudicator and procedure. Justice Alito’s fiscal-exposure concern may explain why Congress might have imposed a time bar, but it cannot justify extending § 3702(b)(1) beyond its textual scope to a separate, later-enacted remedial scheme.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s best point is the Babcock-inspired caution against finding displacement of § 3702 absent a clear substitute, coupled with § 3702(a)(1)(A)’s broad subject-matter coverage of claims involving retired pay. But that argument does not grapple with the trigger Congress chose for the time bar: § 3702(b)(1) applies only to claims “presented under this section,” and § 1413a directs CRSC requests into a different, statute-specific process with a different decisionmaker and payment mechanism—making it textually unnatural to treat them as “presented under” § 3702. As Justice Barrett notes, this is not an implied repeal case so much as § 3702’s own residual clause (“except as otherwise provided by law”) doing work: § 1413a “otherwise provide[s]” the settlement-like determination (eligibility and amount) that § 3702 would otherwise perform. Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s harmonization proposal effectively rewrites § 3702(b)(1) to cover claims not presented under § 3702, and I cannot adopt that extension based on policy concerns about fiscal exposure rather than enacted text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett press the strongest textual point that § 3702(b)(1) bars only claims “presented under this section,” and that CRSC requests travel through § 1413a’s DoD process. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas that you cannot read § 3702(b) in isolation from § 3702(a)(1)(A)’s subject-matter assignment of “claims involving … retired pay” to the governmentwide settlement framework, which applies unless Congress has clearly “otherwise provided” a substitute regime; § 1413a creates an entitlement and an administrator, but it does not clearly displace § 3702’s timeliness constraint. Babcock, as Roberts and Thomas invoke it, reinforces a cautious institutional approach here: we should not infer unlimited retroactive monetary exposure from statutory silence, especially where Congress knows how to write a limitations rule when it wants to. The best harmonization remains that DoD determines eligibility and computes CRSC under § 1413a, while § 3702 supplies the default six-year presentment bar for monetary claims involving retired pay.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Babcock-based warning against implied displacement is the strongest counter, and I agree we should not infer repeal of a fiscal limitation lightly. But the text of § 3702(b)(1) limits its own reach to claims “presented under this section,” and § 1413a channels CRSC applications to a distinct, statute-specific adjudication by the service Secretaries (eligibility plus amount), which is the operative “settlement” determination—so the claim is not, in ordinary public meaning, presented under § 3702 at all, as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes. Justice Kavanaugh’s harmonization proposal effectively treats § 3702(b) as if it were triggered by subject matter alone, collapsing the “presented under this section” condition and thereby extending the time bar beyond its textual trigger. Babcock remains distinguishable because there Congress had not “otherwise provided” a different settlement decisionmaker; here § 3702(a)(1)(A)’s own carveout (“except as otherwise provided by law”) is satisfied by § 1413a’s affirmative assignment of the determination function to DoD.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s Babcock-based caution seriously: “except as otherwise provided by law” should not be treated as a broad license to evade § 3702’s governmentwide claims-processing norms absent a definite alternative. But here § 1413a is not merely an entitlement; it “otherwise provides” by assigning the service Secretaries, under SecDef procedures, the eligibility and amount determinations that function as the settlement decision, and § 3702(b)(1) textually time-bars only claims “presented under this section,” which CRSC claims are not. Justice Alito’s fiscal-exposure concern cannot justify importing a limitations rule that Congress did not attach to this targeted remedial program, especially where the practical consequence is to foreclose relief for combat-injured retirees based on a time bar triggered only by a different presentment route. On a procedural-fairness and pragmatist reading that still hews to the text, harmonization runs in the other direction: § 1413a supplies the governing channel, and applying § 3702’s bar would override rather than complement Congress’s chosen process.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3702(a)(1)(A) expressly assigns settlement authority (and attendant limitations, including timeliness) for claims involving “retired pay,” and CRSC—once deemed to involve retired pay—falls within that generally applicable regime absent a clear statutory displacement. Nothing in 10 U.S.C. § 1413a clearly makes its internal eligibility/review provisions an exclusive, comprehensive “settlement” mechanism that overrides the Barring Act’s default rules, and this Court has been reluctant to find such displacement by implication. Under United States v. Babcock, 250 U.S. 328 (1919), a specific statute must provide a sufficiently definite, exclusive settlement framework to supersede the Government’s default settlement authority; § 1413a’s administrative procedures do not plainly do so. A narrow ruling adhering to § 3702’s established structure best respects precedent and preserves institutional stability while leaving any adjustment of timeliness rules to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Barring Act, 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A), establishes a generally applicable settlement regime (including limitations) for “claims involving … retired pay” unless “another law” supplies a truly separate settlement mechanism; nothing in the text of 10 U.S.C. § 1413a clearly displaces that default or speaks to overriding § 3702’s timeliness rules. As an originalist and textualist, I will not infer an implied repeal or displacement of a broad, expressly applicable claims-settlement statute absent a clear statement, and § 1413a’s eligibility/administrative review provisions do not unmistakably create an exclusive settlement scheme for monetary claims against the United States. Because CRSC is treated as involving military retired pay, it falls within § 3702’s coverage, and the Federal Circuit’s application of the Barring Act is consistent with that text. Any broader retroactivity remedy must come from Congress, not judicial implication from § 1413a’s administrative framework.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of the Barring Act assigns settlement authority for claims involving “retired pay” and imposes a six-year limit, 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A), and Congress did not clearly displace that default regime in § 1413a. Section 1413a creates an entitlement and directs the Secretary of Defense (and implementing departments) to administer eligibility and payment, but it does not expressly provide an alternative “settlement” scheme that purports to override § 3702’s timeliness and settlement framework. Under ordinary textualist principles, a specific benefits statute does not impliedly repeal a generally applicable claims-processing and time-bar statute absent a clear conflict or unmistakable displacement, and applying § 3702 here avoids practical consequences of open-ended fiscal exposure and uncertainty in military pay administration. The Federal Circuit’s conclusion in Soto that CRSC claims are claims involving retired pay governed by the Barring Act is therefore the sounder reading.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1413a creates a specific, self-contained entitlement and decision structure for CRSC—authorizing the Secretary of Defense to prescribe procedures and the service Secretaries to adjudicate eligibility and payments—functioning as an administrative determination of the amount due (i.e., a “settlement” mechanism) distinct from the Barring Act’s default regime in 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A). Applying the settled canon that specific statutory schemes control over general ones, § 1413a’s targeted remedial process for combat-injured retirees should displace § 3702’s default settlement authority and associated time limits where they conflict. The Federal Circuit’s contrary approach in Soto v. United States undervalues how Congress structured CRSC to ensure practical access to compensation for a particularly vulnerable population and risks foreclosing meritorious claims on technical timeliness grounds inconsistent with the statute’s remedial aim. Because Congress designed § 1413a to be administered within the military departments with defined review procedures, it supplies the relevant settlement path for CRSC claims even if the claim is characterized as involving “retired pay.”

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3702 is expressly a default regime for “settlement” of monetary claims only where another statute does not provide the relevant administrative determination, and this Court has defined “settlement” as “the administrative determination of the amount due.” 10 U.S.C. § 1413a does just that: it assigns eligibility and administration to the military departments under Secretary-of-Defense procedures and ties payment to specified statutory criteria—i.e., it supplies an internal mechanism to determine entitlement and compute amounts, making the Barring Act’s overlay (including its six-year limit) a poor textual fit. Reading § 3702 to control despite § 1413a’s specific, self-contained scheme would invert the ordinary canon that the specific governs the general and create workability problems by importing an external limitations regime Congress did not attach to CRSC. Consistent with Nat’l Cable & Telecommunications Ass’n v. Gulf Power Co., the more specific CRSC statute should control where applying the Barring Act would conflict with the statute’s assigned decisionmaker and procedures.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Barring Act’s settlement and time-bar provisions apply only to claims “presented under this section,” 31 U.S.C. § 3702(b)(1), and Congress in 10 U.S.C. § 1413a assigned eligibility determinations and implementing procedures for CRSC to the Secretary of Defense and the military departments, indicating a distinct, statute-specific administrative settlement scheme. Reading § 3702(a)(1)(A) to reimpose its default settlement regime (and six-year bar) despite § 1413a’s tailored decisionmaker-and-procedure structure risks rewriting the limitation in § 3702(b) beyond its textual trigger and diluting Congress’s specific allocation of authority. Consistent with the specific-governs-general canon, see Nat’l Cable & Telecomms. Ass’n v. Gulf Power Co., 534 U.S. 327, 335 (2002), § 1413a should control for CRSC claims even if they relate to “retired pay,” and nothing in § 1413a’s text clearly incorporates § 3702’s settlement apparatus. This resolution also respects separation of powers by enforcing Congress’s chosen decisionmaker rather than defaulting to a general claims-processing statute absent a clear textual command.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: CRSC claims, once deemed to involve “retired pay,” fall within the Barring Act’s default settlement framework, which assigns settlement authority and a six-year timeliness limitation to claims involving retired pay. 10 U.S.C. § 1413a establishes eligibility criteria and an administrative determination process, but it does not clearly supply an exclusive “settlement mechanism” that displaces 31 U.S.C. § 3702’s generally applicable procedures and limits. Under the Court’s strong presumption against implied repeal or displacement, a specific statute does not override a general one absent a clear congressional directive, and the better reading is to harmonize § 1413a with § 3702 rather than treat § 1413a as silently superseding the Barring Act. That approach follows the institutional interest in a workable, predictable claims-settlement regime and avoids expanding monetary exposure to the United States without clear statutory authorization.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Barring Act’s limitations apply to claims “presented under this section,” and its six-year bar yields where “another law” provides otherwise. 31 U.S.C. § 3702(b)(1), (b)(1)(A). Section 1413a is not merely substantive; it assigns CRSC eligibility determinations and review to the military departments under procedures promulgated by the Secretary of Defense, indicating Congress supplied a specific, self-contained administrative mechanism for determining and correcting CRSC entitlements rather than routing them through the Barring Act’s default settlement regime. Under the textual canon that the specific governs the general when the schemes address the same subject, § 1413a’s targeted process should control over § 3702’s general settlement framework, and nothing in § 1413a’s text suggests Congress meant its process to be subordinate to GAO’s default procedures. Cf. Nat’l Cable & Telecomms. Ass’n v. Gulf Power Co., 534 U.S. 327, 335 (2002).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1413a is “otherwise provided by law” within the meaning of 31 U.S.C. § 3702(a)(1)(A) because it assigns the Secretary concerned the responsibility to determine CRSC eligibility and calculate the monthly amount due, i.e., to make the administrative determination that constitutes “settlement” of the claim. Reading the Barring Act’s default settlement/time-bar regime to override that tailored process would undercut Congress’s targeted remedial scheme for combat-disabled retirees and produce the practical consequence of systematically reducing benefits through a limitations rule not expressed in § 1413a. The Federal Circuit’s approach in Soto v. United States treats the Barring Act as controlling even where a later, specific benefits statute directs who decides entitlement and how amounts are determined, which is difficult to reconcile with § 3702’s own “except as otherwise provided by law” clause and basic specificity/canon principles. Given the statute’s structure and the equities for medically retired combat veterans, procedural fairness and practical consequences favor recognizing § 1413a’s self-contained mechanism as displacing § 3702’s default limits for CRSC determinations.
